{id === 'whiteout' && <>

Start with ground insulation

A sleeping bag and a sleeping pad do different jobs. Your body compresses insulation beneath you; a pad adds resistance to heat flowing into the ground. Compare documented R-values for the exact model rather than thickness or cinematic artwork. The NeoAir XTherm NXT profile explains the manufacturer’s 7.3 R-value and the unresolved retailer variant. An R-value is not a minimum safe air temperature.

Build a complete winter sleep system

Match pad width and length to your body and sleeping position. Keep your sleeping bag, spare layers and ground insulation dry. Check the bag’s documented temperature rating and the assumptions behind it; a pad does not replace clothing, shelter or a suitable bag. Practise assembling the full system near an easy exit before taking it into remote winter conditions.

Plan shelter and a way back

Check the forecast and local travel advisories before leaving. Agree on a route, turnaround criteria and an overdue contact plan. Shelter must address wind and precipitation as well as ground insulation. Carry accessible lighting and communication appropriate to your location; see the lighting and charging guide and navigation and communication plan. A survival-themed product image does not establish a safe expedition limit.

Inspect, repair and prepare a backup

Inflate the pad and inspect the valve and seams before travel. Clear sharp debris from the sleeping area and follow the manufacturer’s care instructions. Carry a compatible repair kit and know how to use it. Plan what you will do if an inflatable pad leaks, wet gear cannot be dried or conditions exceed your equipment and experience. Avoid flames and unvented combustion inside shelters.
